sentences.text: MFA No.9420/2011 is filed by the claimant seeking enhancement of compensation.
MFA No.1694/2011 is filed by the insurance company on the ground that the offending vehicle was not involved in the accident and also for reducing the quantum of compensation.

Brief facts:
2. On 30.12.2008, at about 9.30 p.m., the claimant herein had been to Pandavapura,
on his motor bike bearing No.KA-11-K-6546, and while he was returning to his home town Ballenahally on Pandavapura- Srirangapatna Main Road, he met with an accident, hit by tractor bearing No.KA-13-T-1554 and trailer bearing No.KA-13-T-1555, which came from Srirangapatna side towards Pandavapura side,
due to impact the claimant had sustained injuries over his head, chest, right leg and over his back.
3. Hence, a claim petition was filed by the appellant-claimant under Section-166 of the M.V. Act,
claiming compensation for the injuries suffered in the accident.

The Tribunal on appreciating the materials on record, allowed the claim petition in part, and awarded a compensation of Rs.11,95,850/-, along with interest at 9% per annum from the date of petition till the date of realisation.
The Tribunal held respondent No.2 therein, liable to pay the compensation.
4. Heard arguments of the learned counsel for the parties and perused the materials on record.

REGARDING LIABILITY :
5. The learned counsel for the appellant - insurance company submitted that tractor bearing No.KA- 13-T-1554 and trailer bearing No.KA-13-T-1555, was not involved in the accident, but it was implicated for the purpose of claim.
Therefore, argued with reference to the evidence and submitted that the said tractor/trailer is not involved in the accident.
Further, submitted that the quantum awarded is on higher side and prays to reduce.
6. On the other hand, the learned counsel for the claimant submitted that the quantum of compensation awarded is on lesser side and prays to increase the same.

7. In the claim petition, it is alleged that the tractor bearing No.KA-13-T-1554 and trailer bearing No.KA-13-T-1555 had hit the claimant, while the claimant was riding on his motor bike No.KA-11-K-6546.

The accident had occurred on 30.12.2008 at 9.30 p.m., a complaint before Police was lodged on 31.12.2008 at afternoon about 3.00 p.m.
8.

The learned counsel for the insurance company submitted that in the wound certificate at Exhibit-P4, it is stated that there was road traffic accident and the claimant was hit by unknown vehicle and it was a 'hit and run' case.

Therefore, only on this medical documentary evidence, the insurance company's contends that at an initial point of time, it was given before the hospital authorities that it was a hit and run case without mentioning the number of the tractor, but subsequently a National Insurance Co Ltd vs Sri B M Mahendra on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135993793/

10. In the hospital records, it is revealed that it is a road traffic accident case.
If the complaint before the Police has been lodged after some considerable point of - 11 - time, then the doubt expressed by the learned counsel for the insurance company would have been accepted.
But considering the chronological time of event, the date and time of the accident, lodging of the complaint before the Police all within a reasonable period of time.
11. Admittedly, the claimant was unconscious after the accident, as he suffered serious head injury.
Just because the nature of the vehicle and number is not stated in the hospital records, that cannot alone be doubted regarding the involvement of the vehicle.

Where reasonable evidence is placed on record, that too within 24 hours from the time of the accident, the complaint lodged before the Police stating the nature of the vehicle and the number, then in the absence of any contra evidence the said complaint cannot be doubted.
Even though PW-1 may not be eye-witness but PW-2 is eye-witness to the accident and he is admitted to the hospital.
12. But PW-2 has stated that in the complaint that a tractor/trailer hit the claimant.

Therefore,
- 12 - considering these chronological events occurred as above discussed and as there is no much time gap between the date and time of the accident and date and time of the reporting the crime to the police, therefore there is no evidence on record to show that there is manipulation of records.

13. Furthermore, upon considering the arguments by the learned counsel for the insurance company that in the motor vehicle report, it is stated that there is no physical damage to the tractor and trailer, but the tractor/trailer is a bigger vehicle.

Even though the tractor/trailer being bigger vehicle had impacted motor cycle, there may be or there may not be chances of causing damage to the tractor/trailer since it is big vehicle, but the right side indicator of the motor cycle in question was National Insurance Co Ltd vs Sri B M Mahendra on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135993793/

sentences.text:
The Tribunal should also act with caution, if it proposed to accept the expert evidence of doctors who did not treat the injured but who give `ready to use'
disability certificates, without proper medical assessment.
There are several instances of unscrupulous doctors who without treating the injured, readily giving liberal disability certificates to help the claimants.
But where the disability certificates are given by duly constituted Medical Boards, they may be accepted subject to evidence regarding the genuineness of such certificates.
The Tribunal may invariably make it a point to require the evidence of the Doctor who treated the injured or who assessed the permanent disability.

Mere production of a disability certificate or Discharge Certificate will not be proof of the extent of disability stated therein unless the Doctor who treated the claimant or who medically examined and assessed the extent of disability of claimant, is tendered for cross- examination with reference to the certificate.

If the Tribunal is not satisfied with the medical evidence produced by the claimant, it can constitute a Medical Board (from a panel maintained by it in National Insurance Co Ltd vs Sri B M Mahendra on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135993793/

13. We may now summarise the principles discussed above :
(i) All injuries (or permanent disabilities arising from injuries), do not result in loss of earning capacity.
( ii) The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity.

To put it differently, the percentage of loss of earning capacity is not the same as the percentage of permanent disability (except in a few cases, where the Tribunal on the basis of evidence, concludes that percentage of loss of earning capacity is the same as percentage of permanent disability).
(iii) The doctor who treated an injured-claimant or who examined him subsequently to assess the extent of his permanent disability can give evidence only in regard the extent of permanent disability.
The loss of earning capacity is something that will have to be assessed by the Tribunal with reference to the evidence in entirety.

(iv) The same permanent disability may result in different percentages of loss of earning capacity in different persons, depending upon the nature of profession,
occupation or job, age, education and other factors."
The evidence showed that at the time of the accident, the appellant was aged around 25 years and was eking his livelihood as a cheese vendor.
He claimed that he was earning a sum of Rs.3000/- per month.
The Tribunal held that as there was no acceptable evidence of income of the appellant, it should be assessed at Rs.900/- per month as the minimum wage was Rs.891 per month.
It would be very difficult to expect a roadside vendor to have accounts or other documents regarding income.

As the accident occurred in the year 1991, the Tribunal ought to have assumed the income as at least Rs.1500/- per month (at the rate of Rs.50/- per day) or Rs.18,000/- per annum, even in the absence of specific documentary evidence regarding income."
21. The principle of law laid down in the aforesaid judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court regarding permanent physical disability and functional disability is applicable in the present case also.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Just because the nature of the vehicle and number is not stated in the hospital records, that cannot alone be doubted regarding the involvement of the vehicle.

20. The Doctor can only say the physical disability either permanent or temporary, but the functional disability is to be assessed taking into consideration, the nature of injury sustained,
nature of the disability and suffering sustained with respect to the avocation of the claimant.
The claimant was aged 28 years old and was working as storekeeper.
Presently, the claimant is no longer working as a storekeeper due to such - 18 - disability.
There may not be evidence of the doctor that the injured has suffered 100% of permanent physical National Insurance Co Ltd vs Sri B M Mahendra on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135993793/

In the present case, the claimant was working as a storekeeper and due to the injury, the claimant is not able to work as he was working - 21 - earlier.
Therefore, he suffered 100% of functional disability affecting the earning capacity.
Therefore, it is considered in the present case that the claimant has suffered 100% of functional disability.
22. Exhibit-P124 is the salary certificate claiming that the claimant was receiving a salary of Rs.8,000/- but this Exhibit-P124 is just a written paper stated to have been given by the Contractor.
But it is not an authenticate format to prove the pay slip.
Under these circumstances, the notional income is to be taken into consideration.
The accident is of the year 2004.
Therefore the notional income at Rs.4,500/- per month is adopted, since the claimant had suffered 100% functional disability affecting the future prospects in life, therefore as per Division Bench judgment of this Court in the case of New India Assurance Company Ltd., Vs.
